findings.claim: The exam will not ask you about your trip directly, but it will give you an unfamiliar fieldwork scenario ... Examiners expect you to write about your own physical investigation by name
findings.truth: Paper 3 Sections A and B assess the student's own two investigations - the spec says students 'will be assessed on at least two of the six enquiry stages ... across both their investigations' - as well as unfamiliar scenarios. The sentence also contradicts its own second half.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/geography-a-1GA0.md, Component 3 assessment information (lines 2395-2440)

findings.claim: 'examiners reward justified choices'; 'vague answers (we were careful) score zero; specific ones ... score full marks'
findings.truth: No published mark scheme awards zero or full marks on those grounds. These are invented examiner and mark-scheme claims; rewritten as plain advice.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims; spec gives no such rule

findings.claim: Random sampling means stopping every fifth passer-by; systematic sampling means standing at fixed sites
findings.truth: Reversed. Stopping every fifth passer-by is systematic sampling (a fixed interval rule). Random sampling gives every person an equal chance of selection, normally by random numbers. Lesson 1's own glossary defines random sampling correctly, so the unit contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: spec Investigative skills: 'consider appropriate sampling procedures (systematic vs random vs stratified)' (line ~2503); lesson 1 glossary

findings.claim: 'Examiners reward students who name a fix, not just complain about bias'; 'Naming a specific fix in the exam scores higher than complaining about bias'
findings.truth: Invented examiner and mark claims; rewritten as plain advice.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: 'Examiners use the formula TEA'; 'Vague comments ... score nothing'; 'if you don't reference figures, the maximum is half marks'
findings.truth: TEA is a teaching mnemonic, not an examiner formula, and no mark scheme caps a describe answer at half marks for omitting figures. Rewritten as plain advice.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims; spec assessment information

findings.claim: The UK's population reached around 68 million in 2025 and is forecast to pass 73 million by 2050 (repeated in the key fact, practice Q1 and flashcard 1)
findings.truth: ONS mid-2024 estimate is 69.28 million. ONS 2022-based national population projections put the UK at 72.5 million by mid-2032 and 76.6 million by mid-2047, so 73 million is reached in the early 2030s, not 2050.
findings.evidence: ONS National population projections: 2022-based (ons.gov.uk bulletin); Wikipedia Demography of the United Kingdom (ONS mid-2024 estimate 69,281,437)

findings.claim: Each extra person consumes about 500 m3 of water ... per year
findings.truth: About ten times too high. UK average domestic use is about 150 litres per person per day, which is roughly 55 m3 a year. Even total per-capita abstraction is well under 200 m3.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Water supply and sanitation in the United Kingdom: average urban use 150 L/person/day; recomputation 150 x 365 = 54,750 L = 54.75 m3

findings.claim: over 30% of new car sales were electric in 2024 (repeated in flashcard 2 and in practice Q4's data and mark scheme)
findings.truth: Battery electric cars were 19.6% of new UK car registrations in 2024. All plug-ins together (BEV + PHEV) were 28.2%, still under 30%. Practice Q4 recomputed at 20%: 1,950,000 x 0.20 = 390,000.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Electric car use by country (UK plug-in share 28.2% in 2024); recomputation of the mark scheme

findings.claim: The exam will reward students who can name both scales.
findings.truth: Invented exam-reward claim; rewritten as plain advice.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: regions such as the North East, Wales and parts of Northern Ireland have GDP per head only 60-70% of the UK average
findings.truth: ONS 2023 regional GDP per head: UK 39,845 pounds; North East 28,583 (72%); Wales 29,316 (74%); Northern Ireland 32,944 (83%). The true gap is about a quarter, not 30-40%.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, List of regions of the United Kingdom by GDP (ONS regional GDP per head, 2023)

findings.claim: Net migration to the UK was around 685,000 in 2023 (the latest full year), a record level (repeated in the key fact, the takeaways, knowledge check 4 and flashcard 9)
findings.truth: 685,000 was a provisional ONS estimate that was later revised sharply upward. The record is 944,000 in the year ending March 2023, and net migration has since fallen steeply, to about 204,000 in the year ending June 2025. The lesson's own point about revision makes the stale headline worse.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Modern immigration to the United Kingdom, citing ONS long-term international migration series

findings.claim: Examiners reward candidates who can link two parts of the spec
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim; rewritten as plain advice.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: The 2014 Medmerry managed-realignment scheme ... removed 7 km of crumbling sea wall and let the tide return (repeated in flashcard 7)
findings.truth: Medmerry was completed in 2013. Managed realignment there built new flood embankments inland and then breached the old shingle sea defence; no 7 km of sea wall was removed. The 7 km figure belongs to the new inland defences.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Selsey (Medmerry scheme, completed 2013: new defences built inland, intertidal area formed seaward)

findings.claim: Spelling, punctuation and grammar count for an extra 4 marks on this paper
findings.truth: SPaG sits inside the 64 raw marks, not on top of them: 'Of the 64 raw marks available, up to 4 marks are awarded for spelling, punctuation, grammar and use of specialist terminology.'
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/geography-a-1GA0.md, Component 3 assessment overview (lines 348-380) and assessment information

findings.claim: The six stages of the enquiry process are: 1) formulate questions, 2) choose methods, 3) collect data, 4) present and process, 5) analyse and conclude, 6) evaluate (flashcard 1 gives a matching six-item list)
findings.truth: The spec's own six enquiry stages are: 1 kinds of question and enquiry processes; 2 techniques and methods used in fieldwork; 3 processing and presenting data; 4 analysing and explaining data; 5 drawing evidenced conclusions; 6 reflecting critically. The lesson inserts 'collect data' as a stage and merges analyse with conclude. Options: (a) relabel content and flashcard to the spec's six stages, or (b) leave, since the exam never asks students to number a stage. Blocker for (a): the flashcard answer is inherently a comma list, which the validator rejects, so the flashcard would need rewording as well. Recommend (a) with the flashcard question changed to 'Which stage of the enquiry process comes after processing and presenting data?'
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/geography-a-1GA0.md lines 2415-2440
findings.ruling: Leave: needs a source check or a ripple through keyed answers (relabel queue).

findings.claim: Rural areas, where over 90% of journeys are by car, find it hard to switch
findings.truth: National Travel Survey data put car driver plus passenger at roughly three-quarters to four-fifths of trips in rural villages and hamlets; over 90% holds only for distance travelled, not trips. Recommend softening to 'about four in five rural trips are by car' once someone checks the current NTS table; I could not fetch NTS in this session.
findings.evidence: no verified source fetched
findings.ruling: Leave: needs a source check or a ripple through keyed answers (relabel queue).

findings.claim: schemes like the 200 million pound National Cycle Network expansion
findings.truth: I found no published 200 million pound National Cycle Network programme. The verifiable national figure is the 2 billion pound active-travel package announced in 2020. Recommend replacing the figure with that package, or dropping the number and keeping 'investment in the National Cycle Network'.
findings.evidence: no verified source found
findings.ruling: Leave: needs a source check or a ripple through keyed answers (relabel queue).

findings.claim: National Parks: 15 in the UK, covering around 8% of the country
findings.truth: The 15 parks total about 23,000 km2 of a UK land area of about 242,000 km2, roughly 9.5%; the usual published figure is about 10%. Not mark-affecting.
findings.evidence: recomputation from published park areas

findings.claim: What is the minimum useful sample size for a questionnaire survey? Around 50 respondents
findings.truth: There is no official minimum sample size in the spec or in any mark scheme. The content's softer framing ('50 questionnaires give a much more reliable picture than 10') is fine; the flashcard turns it into a rule.
findings.evidence: spec Investigative skills: 'consider appropriate sampling procedures ... and sample size'

findings.claim: The Campaign to Protect Rural England estimates 290,000 homes are planned on Green Belt land by 2026
findings.truth: CPRE's State of the Green Belt reporting has published figures near 258,000 homes on land released from the Green Belt, and does not attach a 2026 deadline. I could not verify 290,000; left unchanged.
findings.evidence: no verified source fetched

findings.claim: median weekly earnings in London were 853 pounds in 2023, against 629 pounds in the North East
findings.truth: Plausible against ASHE 2023 but not verified in this session. Left unchanged.
findings.evidence: no verified source fetched

findings.claim: Around 5.7 million UK properties are at flood risk
findings.truth: Environment Agency figures are for England, not the UK, and have moved: the long-used figure was 5.2 million; the 2024 National Flood Risk Assessment raised it to about 6.3 million. Sources conflict, so left unchanged.
findings.evidence: no single settled figure verified

findings.claim: By the 2070s ... winters 25% wetter. Sea level around London could rise 0.7-1.0 m
findings.truth: UKCP18 headlines are 'up to 35% wetter' winters by 2070 under high emissions, and London sea-level rise of about 0.5-1.15 m by 2100 rather than by the 2070s. The lesson's numbers are inside the plausible spread but mislabelled; not verified in this session.
findings.evidence: no source fetched

findings.claim: Bus franchising in Greater Manchester (Bee Network, 2024)
findings.truth: The first franchised Bee Network buses ran in September 2023 and franchising was completed in January 2025. The bare '2024' is a midpoint, not a start date.
findings.evidence: widely reported roll-out dates; not fetched

findings.claim: Met Office records show annual mean temperature rose by about 1.0 C between 1981-2010 and 2014-2023
findings.truth: Against the 1981-2010 baseline the rise is nearer 0.7-0.8 C; the Met Office headline is that 2014-2023 was 1.25 C warmer than 1961-1990. Baseline mismatch rather than a wrong number.
findings.evidence: Met Office State of the UK Climate framing; not fetched this session

summary: Fieldwork technique and exam-structure teaching is mostly sound, but lesson 2 reverses random and systematic sampling, and the UK challenge statistics in lessons 4-6 are stale or invented: the population projection, per-person water use, the 2024 EV share, regional GDP per head, the net migration headline and the Medmerry scheme were all wrong. A run of fabricated examiner and mark-scheme claims across five lessons was rewritten as plain advice.
